question.:question/problem: Calculate $F(x)$ given that $f(x)={x}^{4}$ and ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=4$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4+1}}{4+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C) &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ &= \frac{1}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5})+0 \\ &= \frac{1}{5}\cdot 5{x}^{4} \\ &= {x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{∂D}-3y\,dx+2x\,dy,
$$ where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-3y$ and $Q(x,y)=2x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}-3y\,dx+2x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(-3))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}5\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =5\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =5\cdot ({4}^{2}-\frac{2\cdot 2}{2}) \\  & =5\cdot (16-2) \\  & =5\cdot 14 \\  & =70.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F=\left(\left(3 x + 2 y\right)^{2}\right)\,i+\left(\left(3 x + 4 y\right)^{2}\right)\,j.$ 
Evaluate $\nabla\cdot F$ at the point $(2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=\nabla\cdot F=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

When differentiating $P$ with respect to $x$, hold $y$ constant; when differentiating $Q$ with respect to $y$, hold $x$ constant.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla\cdot F & =\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \\  & =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\left(3 x + 2 y\right)^{2})+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\left(3 x + 4 y\right)^{2}) \\  & =18 x + 12 y+\left(24 x + 32 y\right) \\  & =2 \left(21 x + 22 y\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\nabla\cdot F)(2,1) & =44 (1) + 42 (2) \\ & =48+\left(80\right) \\ & =128.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral

$$
\oint_C(y + \sin{\left(x \right)})\,dx+(2 x + \cos{\left(y \right)})\,dy\,?
$$

The cross partials are $\partial P/\partial y=1$ and $\partial Q/\partial x=2$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/0a/0a8351f5cdfa59df7ec8a328c18b6e83342796728e11ff26911ce661eda1513b.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y + \sin{\left(x \right)}$ and $Q(x,y)=2 x + \cos{\left(y \right)},$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=1,\qquad\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=2.
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C(y + \sin{\left(x \right)})\,dx+(2 x + \cos{\left(y \right)})\,dy&=\iint_D(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y})\,dA\\&=\iint_D\left(2-\left(1\right)\right)\,dA\\&=\iint_D\left(1\right)\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 3,\ 0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D\left(1\right)\,dA&=\iint_\Delta\left(1\right)r\,dr\,d\theta\\&=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{3}r\,dr\,d\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}+2x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x+2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (6x+2) \\  & =\frac{6x+2}{2\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={\left(\frac{6x+2}{2\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+2x}}\right)|}_{x=-1} \\  & =\frac{6(-1)+2}{2\sqrt{3(-1)^{2}+2(-1)}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
